title: Our dream was to release our own games but in 2026, everyone is doing it. Is it even worth it anymore?
author: Speccy_G
selftext:
My brother and I spent the past six months building a game. The reaction we keep running into is that it looks like something that got generated rather than made, so I wanted to lay out what's actually in it.

The game is called Colony Battle Arena and is available on Steam and the App Store.

The game genre is RTS but with one catch: there’s no economy to manage and nothing you can build. Your army spawns on its own, and everything you do is about commanding it. You farm up off your kills, get stronger as the match goes on, and win by destroying the enemy base. Eight teams are dropped into one arena.

Since we call it an RTS, people assume they'll be gathering resources. If we call it a MOBA, which it plays like in the sense that you must destroy your enemies base they come expect playing as a hero and not commanding an army. We end up sending everyone in the wrong direction before they've even seen it.

We've got a server running for online ranked matches, and the game's available on Steam as a paid release and free on iOS.

We used AI in production, and I'm not going to try to hide that fact. It helped with asset generation and a lot of the tooling, and it's a big part of how two casual modders shipped a full game like this at all.

The design, the systems, the netcode, and the balance came out of a plan we'd been sketching for over a year. People still assume it was a one-shot prompt by Claude.

The plan from here is community first. We want a real player base before we worry much about revenue. The game is free on mobile with ads. But ad revenue only works at scale, which means our actual job for the next year is getting people in and keeping them playing. The dream is that one day, it’ll become profitable.

The thing I'd most like input on is the explanation problem. 

If you've shipped something that doesn't sit in an existing category, how did you get people interested in it and to understand it? Guess lots of vibe coders will be asking themselves the same question right now.

Is it even worth it?

comments.author: aigamedev-mod
comments.body: u/Speccy_G please add details on how AI was used to make this. Just stating that you used AI doesn't pass the rule. The community is a dev community, add dev details. Rule 4 is there to make sure promotional posts contribute by getting into the process and actual development. There's a real risk of the sub being swamped by self-promotion. If you don't update, this post may be removed.

replies.author: Brave-History-6502
replies.body: Thank you for moderating this sub.

comments.author: fighthonor
comments.body: Just releasing a game is not enough. You need some sort of marketing plan to get exposure.

replies.author: Speccy_G
replies.body: We are relying on both organic social media posting on Instagram and TikTok and paid ads. The videos that we post on social media are used for our paid Meta ads too. For iOS, we are buying search recommendations through Apple ads. We briefly ran Google ads as well, but that got expensive quickly, so we ended up indefinitely suspending that campaign. Our Steam sales are still quite low for the budget we have already burned through. Next we want to address our Steam and App Store pages to fix up the game content we show there. Clearly people aren’t convinced. Our steam page had 26k views and 24 downloads so far. Since iOS is free, we had a bit more success there with 85 users since 01.11.2026 but overall, it is all looking a bit underwhelming so far.

comments.author: Pilgrim_91
comments.body:
I’d say game development at whole isn’t worth it, and never has been. And you’re making an online game, which makes your goal 100x times harder. And you’re making an RTS, which means that you’ll face a very demanding fan base. Like you deliberately chose “Nightmare” difficulty for your first project.

As for what you can do - run some playtests to find out if the game is fun (hard to judge by the video, but it didn’t sell me the game at all). Talk to your brother and make a decision whether you believe in this idea or have something better. Maybe you’ll just add this project to your portfolio and switch to another one. Maybe you’ll try to save this one, find a publisher or invest into marketing yourselves, switch off ads until the playerbase gets critical mass. Both options can be successful, both options can fail. Chances of failure are much higher, and always have been.

And here we’re back to the starting point: you don’t become a game developer (especially indie game dev) to be successful, you become a game developer only if you can’t live without it.

Good luck with whatever choice you make!

replies.author: Speccy_G
replies.body: Thanks for the insights! As the title says, we started with a dream but it seems like the indie community is quite hostile, and especially those devs have very negative attitudes towards ai. They are often the first to tell you why your vision isn’t going to succeed. We got inspired by a custom scenario for Age Of Empires 2 many years ago and always wanted a game like this to come back so we built something heavily inspired by it. But as you stated, it’s a tough genre and we’ve put ourselves into this position. With GTA 6 also looming around the corner, we sort of knew what we were getting into and still decided to commit. I am curious how other developers are doing in similar circumstances.

replies.author: greentrillion
replies.body: Looks pretty boring and slow. Really hard to compete with classics like AOE and SC. Even new attemps at buidling RTS games by bigger studios have failed because the AOE and SC are just too good and everything pales in comparison. You can basically do your game as a custom game in SC2 or Warcraft and have a much better experience which is why RTS is a bad genre for you because RTS takes a lot of skill and focus to play. It's not for casuals.

comments.author: Intelligent-Cap-8886
comments.body: Write for yourself. Its that easy. Write the game you want to play. If you succeed, you got a new game to play. Anyone else also liking it is a bonus that you dont have to care about.

comments.author: ManduLaboratory
comments.body: Nice project! One thing I noticed: the hit feedback feels a bit weak, so shooting and getting hit don't feel very satisfying yet. Maybe some hit flashes, particles or screen shake would help. and also need more hit feedback animations too.

replies.author: Speccy_G
replies.body: Thanks! In a game centred on combat that surely is something we should polish more. The challenge with that is going to be the extra load it will bring when applied to 1600 units at peak population in a match. We wanted the game to run on mobile and it already drops below 25fps on an iPhone 16 Pro. But we will definitely look into it. Tier up animations, the progress bar, brighter more diverse map and improvements to unit animations are at the top of our list for the first update since our launch.

comments.author: Glittering-Kick-7251
comments.body: Game sounds like the zergling blood custom map in starcraft I played as a kid. so I'll give it a try. I know there's a big hate against AI currently but it will pass with time so I'd say keep at it.

replies.author: Speccy_G
replies.body: I never played StarCraft, but I’d imagine the Age of Empires custom blood map this was inspired by was itself borrowing ideas from the StarCraft community maps that were popular around the same time. The younger crowd may not be familiar with such concepts at all, but I think you’ll feel right at home playing it. We hope to bring the fun of old blood maps to a modern audience on modern platforms and contribute to the genre’s potential comeback.

replies.author: Glittering-Kick-7251
replies.body:
Sounds awesome. Also regarding the AI and game dev, there's a flood of games made with AI but only a few that stands out. A lot of the games are barebones or "demos" so a full complete game of good quality will definitely stand out.

Also in Asia, people don't hate on AI use as much as Western countries so there's still a strong audience for games made with AI.

comments.author: Vivid-Snow-2089
comments.body:
gamedev always was done for the love of it, it was never 'worth it' from a get rich perspective...

most people's ideas aren't unique or special enough to become one of the big winners...

but the fact that there ARE standout games and real winners is what propels people to keep trying and throwing stuff, and that inspiration is why so many ideas get tested and tried and we as society validate or bury them via financial incentives...

except some people are financially secure to the point they don't have to be economically 'viable' and those can produce some of the most unique, ambitious, and crazy/zany ideas (along with trash)

AI has collapsed the effort/time requirement for testing ideas so now we see a lot more landing.... between people looking to easily grift financial wins to peopel spamming out one prompt garbage and calling it groundbreaking... we certainly have an era of excess things to look at and no good discoverability solution for it since our systems are still based on the human rate of labor/development without ai assistance

comments.author: deliosenvy
comments.body:
Sorry to disappoint you mate but game-dev was never worth it. EVER. In the tech field it was the most grueling and financially disappointing part. You could do everything right and still fail hard, because pressure is from both financing/time investment and extremely art-form sensitive end-user community.

And today if you make a relatively successful game someone else will just copy it.

comments.author: Heath_co
comments.body: What was possible is now easy. But what is now hard was once impossible.

replies.author: Speccy_G

comments.author: Fearless-Relentless
comments.body:
yeah what the video describe is just MOBA, It is just like tower defense. just start attacking and defending, the controls is upgrades and placement and control of any special units. and just like LoL and Dota, units jus spawn and action starts.

is it worth it? you have to define what "success" means to you in this game development. not every good product makes money and not every bad product didn't make money. there are phases and context and nuances and environment factors, etc.

a good game with updates (or not) keep people coming back to play. kingdom rush is single player and it is one of the best tower defense game to me. graphics are great, art style, animation is smooth. hero characters, quite fun and have to think for harder levels. simple gameplay and enough to entertain. neither too long or too short to play per game for what it is supposed to be. can be played on mobile and PC. something like this is what i really liked and i definitely want to play the other kingdom rush games after trying the first one, for example.

I don't care if AI is used or not. the game must be fun and engaging. should look good as well. 16 bit era gaming SNES, Sega genesis, even micro genius 8 bit era era, has shown us that simple sprites and low resolutions can look amazing even till today. If AI helps you save time and money, go for it. Game must be of quality
